context: The stack is on the left, with its top above its bottom. The vertical singly linked list on the right has its head at the top and its tail at the bottom, with next arrows pointing down. Between them, a left-pointing arrow is labeled “Linked list implementation / Stack interface.”
description: The top of the stack corresponds to the head node and the bottom to the tail node. Reading the stack from bottom to top therefore gives the reverse of the list’s head-to-tail order. At the opening of the stack on the left, the push arrow points down into the stack and the pop arrow points up and out.

frames.announcement: The initial stack contains four elements. Head node 5 is the top and tail node 1 is the bottom.
frames.explanation: The stack starts with four elements, [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top. The list runs 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail. Head node 5 is the top of the stack and tail node 1 is the bottom.
frames.key_state: The initial stack is [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top. The list runs 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail, with head node 5 at the top of the stack.
frames.title: Initial stack: head node 5 is on top

frames.announcement: The call push(4) inserts node 4 at the head of the list. Node 4 becomes the new head and the top of the stack.
frames.explanation: The call push(4) is labeled “Add node 4 to the front of the list” on the right. The new teal node, 4, goes above the old head node, 5. Its next link points to 5, and 4 becomes the head. The list now runs 4 → 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail. The stack has five elements, [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from bottom to top. Node 4 is the head and the top, while 1 is still the tail and the bottom.
frames.key_state: After push(4), the stack is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from bottom to top. The list runs 4 → 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail. The new head node, 4, is on top.
frames.title: Push 4 at the head of the list

frames.announcement: The call pop() removes and returns head node 4, making 5 the head and the top of the stack again.
frames.explanation: The call pop() is labeled “Remove the head node” on the right. It removes and returns the old head, 4, making its successor, 5, the new head. The list is back to 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail. The stack again has four elements, [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top. Node 5 is the head and the top, while 1 is still the tail and the bottom.
frames.key_state: After pop() removes and returns head node 4, the stack is [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top. The list runs 5 → 2 → 3 → 1 from head to tail, and 5 is back on top.
frames.title: Pop 4 from the head of the list

result: A linked-list stack pushes and pops by adding and removing nodes only at the head of the list. Both operations take O(1) time.
summary: The head of a singly linked list serves as the top of the stack. Both pushes and pops take place at the head.
title: Pushing and popping with a linked list
